Scalability and Welding Effects on the Dynamical Responses of Box Assembly with Removable Component Systems
recent_works.abstract: Scalability of the original test design for the box assembly with removable component (BARC) structure is of interest in the field of experimental structural analysis. As complex structures become increasingly difficult to test experimentally the larger they become, it is a common test practice to use a scaled-down representative model to understand the characteristics of these systems. For complex structures with non-rigid boundary conditions, there exists a gap in understanding the effects of scalability and welding. To gain a better understanding of the outcomes of this phenomenon, the dynamical effects of upscaling the dimensions of the BARC structure are analyzed. Three variations of the BARC are investigated experimentally and computationally, namely, the original BARC system, the BARC system upscaled at 1.5 times the size of the original model, and the BARC system upscaled at two times the size of the original model. The original BARC is tested to investigate the properties of the predetermined boundary conditions. recent_works.title: Comparative Dynamical Study and Repeatability of Metallic Plates Using Additive and Subtractive Manufacturing Techniques
recent_works.abstract: Many times, when components are subjected to harsh operating conditions where the structural integrity of the part is of utmost importance, metal and its alloys are used. However, the high strength and durability of these materials have proved challenging to form into complex geometries. Recent discoveries in the additive manufacturing space allow engineers to harness the true potential of these materials. With this said, research has shown that the final product exhibits variability in its dynamical responses. Before these parts begin to make their way into critical applications, further investigations should be conducted into their dynamical characteristics. This research aims to address the gap in literature by investigating the vibratory properties of “identical” metal components fabricated using traditional and additive manufacturing techniques. This study has four main objectives, two of which are the preliminary findings discussed here. recent_works.title: Impacts of Bolt Preload Variation on the Vibrational Properties of Bolted-Joint Beams
recent_works.abstract: In the aerospace industry, many complex structures that contain several bolted joints are deployed in service environments where they experience harsh conditions. As a result of high amplitude vibrations induced in service, these structures can accumulate imperfections, such as fatigue, wear, and preload loss. Typically, a loss of preload can affect the dynamical properties of structures, so it is essential to understand these effects to predict and mitigate failure in systems. The purpose of this study is to investigate and quantify the effects of varying preloads on the linear and nonlinear vibrational properties of bolted-joint systems. The structure being experimentally tested is the Brake-Reuss beam, which consists of two components that are fastened together at a lap joint using three bolts. Five different torques are tested using free, random, and harmonic excitations. Different levels of excitation are considered in the forced vibration tests to monitor the changes in the beam’s nonlinear behavior across the varying preloads.
